instruction:
Clone the `attack_range_local` repository from `https://github.com/davedittrich/attack_range_local.git` and switch to the `feature/psec` branch. This project uses `python_secrets` (`psec`) for managing configuration secrets.

Initialize a `psec` secrets environment by cloning it from the `secrets.d` directory inside the repository, then generate the required secrets, and apply the default option values. The final state should be a fully configured psec environment with all secrets generated and defaults applied in `~/.secrets/attack_range_local/`.

Generate a GPG key for the identity **Oliver Spryn** with the comment "GitLab GPG Key" and email `[email protected]`. The key should be RSA 4096-bit with no expiration and no passphrase protection.

Write the output to `/app/result.txt`. The file must contain the full output of listing the secret keys in long keyid format, followed by the ASCII-armored public key block for the generated key.

Clone the official Apache Karaf repository to `/app/karaf` and use its built-in Docker build tooling found under `assemblies/docker` to build a multi-platform image for Apache Karaf 4.3.0. The image should support both `linux/arm64` and `linux/arm/v7` platforms and be tagged as `amusarra/karaf:4.3.0`.

The resulting image must be built using Docker's multi-platform build capabilities so that it is usable on both 64-bit and 32-bit ARM devices.

Once the image is built and pushed, inspect the image manifest and write the output to `/app/result.txt`.

A Node.js project is available in `/app`. Run a Node.js development server inside a Docker container that supports live development via a volume mount. The container should use the `node:12-alpine` image, mount the current working directory into `/app` inside the container (set as the working directory), install dependencies, and start the development server. The server must be accessible on host port `3000`, mapped to container port `3000`. The container should run detached so it does not block the terminal.

Clone the `makefile-tutorial` repository from `https://github.com/bureado/makefile-tutorial` into `/app/makefile-tutorial`.

Build the project's `hellomake` binary using Makefile-v5 with a unique GNU build ID embedded (linker flag `--build-id=uuid`). While building, monitor which source files are read from the repository and save that list to `/app/makefile-tutorial/inputs.txt` as Git tree entries.

After building, create a Git ref at `refs/subtrees/<build-id>` in the repository (where `<build-id>` is the GNU build ID extracted from the `hellomake` binary) pointing directly to a tree object — not a commit. That tree object must list exactly the source files that were read during the build (e.g. `Makefile`, `Makefile-v5`, `hellofunc.c`, `hellofunc.h`, `hellomake.c`).

Retrieve build metadata and subtree reference information from a GitHub repository and record it in `/app/result.txt`.

You have a local Git repository at `/app/makefile-tutorial` that has already been configured with a `github` remote and contains subtree references under `refs/subtrees/*`, as well as a compiled binary called `hellomake`. Push those subtree references to the GitHub remote, then clone the repository into a separate read-only working directory. Copy the `hellomake` binary into that clone and use it to extract ELF note information (including the build-id). Append to `/app/result.txt` the output of `readelf -n hellomake`, followed by any `git for-each-ref` entries whose object hash begins with `c17`, followed by the tree listing for the object `4c551e97f288ef0f3a74274e2f24151bdacdefcb`.

The final `/app/result.txt` must contain, in order: the ELF notes section from `hellomake`, the matching ref entries containing `c17`, and the `git ls-tree` output for that specific commit/tree object — all appended sequentially into that single file.

Set up a local Docker registry at `localhost:5000`. Build and push a container image from `https://github.com/wabbit-networks/net-monitor.git#main` to the local registry. Then attach supply chain artifacts to the pushed image using ORAS: attach an SBoM artifact of type `sbom/example` (using `/app/sbom.json` as the artifact file) and a signature artifact of type `signature/example` (using `/app/signature.json` as the artifact file), both referencing the pushed image. After attaching, run `oras discover` to find the referrers of the image and pull one of them back locally.

Once the workflow is complete, write the digest of the pushed image (as output by `docker push`) to `/app/result.txt`. The file should contain only the digest string (e.g., `sha256:<hex>`). Also save the full JSON output of `oras discover` on the pushed image to `/app/discover_output.json`.

Set up a Python virtual environment and install the `pulumi_alicloud` package. Using the installed package, enumerate all classes found within every submodule of `pulumi_alicloud`, and write the results to `/app/result.txt`.

The output file should contain one entry per line, where each line is the fully qualified name in the format `submodule.ClassName` (e.g., `ecs.Instance`). The lines must be sorted alphabetically. The file should include every class discovered across all submodules of the package.

Convert the online CV hosted at `https://p14pall.github.io/online-cv` into a PDF file. The conversion must go through a LaTeX intermediate — the `.tex` file should be located somewhere under `/app/online-cv/`, and the final PDF must be saved at `/app/my-cv.pdf`.

Query the `asterisk` PostgreSQL database to retrieve UCC Premium permission assignments. Specifically, join the `account`, `account2permission`, and `permission` tables to find all accounts where `accounttypeid = 1` and `permissionid = 34`, returning their account ID, login, comment (as name), permission ID, and permission description, ordered by account ID and permission ID.

Write the full query output (including PostgreSQL's default column headers and row count footer) to `/app/result.txt`.

Build and install the E4S Container Layer (e4s-cl) tool from its GitHub repository, configure it with a Singularity backend using the image at `singularity-image/ecp.simg`, and use it to launch an MPI benchmark application. The benchmark to run is `mpi_bench/build/bin/50-bandwidth` with 2 MPI processes via `mpirun`.

The output of the benchmark run must be captured and saved to `/app/result.txt`. This file should contain the standard output produced by the bandwidth benchmark when executed through the e4s-cl launch environment.

Convert the online CV hosted at `https://p18balt.github.io/online-cv-3/` into a PDF file. The resulting PDF should be saved to `/app/cv.pdf`.

The conversion should faithfully render the content of the webpage as a PDF document. You may use any suitable tools or intermediate formats to accomplish this.

A local Tanzu Harbor plugin archive (`tanzu-framework-plugins-registry-allarch.tar.gz`) is available at `~/path/to/cli-for-harbor-go/`. Install the `harbor` plugin from this archive into the local Tanzu CLI.

Once installed, authenticate against the Harbor instance using the credentials file at `/Users/hinl/GolandProjects/cli-for-harbor-go/login-params.yaml`. Then list all Harbor projects twice: once without additional parameters, and once using the parameters file at `/Users/hinl/GolandProjects/cli-for-harbor-go/listprojects-params.yaml`.

Write the combined output to `/app/result.txt`, with the first listing followed by the second listing, concatenated in that order.

Build the `degu` project from source using the repositories at `https://github.com/io-tl/degu-lib` and `https://github.com/io-tl/degu-client`. The build process requires initializing submodules for `degu-lib`, generating a keypair (placing the output in `/tmp/degu-lib/keys.h`), and producing a production build of the final library.

The completed build should result in a compiled shared library or binary artifact in `/tmp/degu-lib/` as produced by the production `make` invocation (with `PROD=yes`). All intermediate source repositories and generated files should reside under `/tmp/`.

Generate a configuration form for the `backend_rocks` custom Drupal module using Drush's code generation capabilities. The module already exists at `web/modules/custom/backend_rocks/`.

The generated configuration form should be associated with the `backend_rocks.settings` config object, accessible at the route `/admin/config/system/backend_rocks`, require the `administer site configuration` permission, have a page title of "Backend Rocks settings", and be placed under the `system.admin_config_system` menu item. The form should be named "Settings". After generation, clear the Drupal caches so the new form and route are recognized by the system.

Use the `rows` CLI tool (install from the `turicas/rows` GitHub repository, `develop` branch) to import CSV data into PostgreSQL. A semicolon-delimited CSV file encoded in Latin-1 is located at `/app/Downloads/receitas_candidatos_doador_originario_2022_BRASIL.csv`. A PostgreSQL database is available via the `$DATABASE_URL` environment variable.

Import the uncompressed CSV file into a table named `receita_2022`, using an all-text schema and the appropriate dialect and encoding settings. Then compress the CSV file in place (producing `/app/Downloads/receitas_candidatos_doador_originario_2022_BRASIL.csv.gz`) and import the compressed version into a second table named `receita_2022_2`, using the same schema, encoding, and dialect settings. Both tables should be present in the database and populated with the imported data upon completion.

Set up a Redis + Trino environment using the `redis-sql` repository from GitHub (https://github.com/redis-field-engineering/redis-sql). The environment should have a RediSearch index named `beers` created on hash keys with the prefix `beer:`, with fields: `id` (TAG SORTABLE), `brewery_id` (TAG SORTABLE), `name` (TEXT SORTABLE). Populate the index by importing beer data from `https://storage.googleapis.com/jrx/beers.json` into Redis.

Once the data is loaded and the Trino connector is configured to query RediSearch, execute the query `SELECT * FROM beers LIMIT 10` against the `redisearch` catalog and `default` schema using Trino. Write the full output of that query to `/app/result.txt`.

Compile Python 3.9.1 from source on this Debian system. The build should result in a working `python3.9` executable installed on the system.

Once the build and installation are complete, write the output of `python3.9 --version` to `/app/result.txt`. The file should contain the version string exactly as reported by the interpreter (e.g., `Python 3.9.1`).

Demonstrate a Lightning Network penalty transaction scenario using Bitcoin Core and Core Lightning (CLN) in regtest mode.

Set up two CLN nodes (L1 and L2) connected to a shared regtest Bitcoin network. Open a funded channel between them. Before any payments, snapshot L1's database and HSM secret into a backup (L1B). After making a payment from L1 to L2, use the stale backup (L1B) to force-close the channel — this broadcasts an outdated commitment transaction. L2 should detect the breach and sweep all channel funds via the penalty mechanism.

Once the penalty sweep is confirmed on-chain, write the following result files:

- `/app/result_l2_funds.json` — the JSON output of L2's `listfunds` after the sweep (confirmed outputs should total approximately 10,000,000,000 msat)
- `/app/result_l1_funds.json` — the JSON output of L1's `listfunds` (should show no confirmed on-chain outputs after the penalty)
- `/app/result_l2_illegal_close.txt` — text from L2's node state confirming it detected the illegal close (must contain the word "illegal")
- `/app/result_penalty_complete.txt` — a marker file confirming the scenario ran to completion

Create a C program at `/app/fork_posix.c` that demonstrates POSIX process creation using `fork()`. The program should spawn a child process: the child process prints its PID information and then executes the `yes` utility (located at `/usr/bin/yes`), while the parent process prints its child's PID, waits for the child to complete, prints "Child Complete", and then sleeps for 50 seconds before exiting. If `fork()` fails, the program should print an error message to stderr.

Compile the program into an executable at `/app/soleh` with execute permissions for all users. Once compilation succeeds, write the text `/app/soleh compiled successfully` to `/app/result.txt`.

Using the miniconda3-3.9-4.12.0 pyenv environment, create two separate conda virtual environments and install `scipy` in each using different solvers.

In the first environment, named `normal`, install `scipy` using the default classic conda solver. After the installation is complete, deactivate and delete this environment, then clean the conda package cache. In the second environment, named `experimental`, install `scipy` using the experimental libmamba solver (via the `--experimental-solver=libmamba` option). The `experimental` environment should remain active with `scipy` successfully installed when the task is complete.

Extract the contents of a RAR archive and place the resulting file at `/app/text.txt`. The archive should contain a file named `text.txt`, and its contents should be present at `/app/text.txt` after extraction.

Retrieve the list of connected instances from a running Tarantool cluster and save the output to `/app/result.txt`.

A Tarantool instance is configured and can be started using the configuration file and source files available in `~/sources/MRG/tarantool`. The instance should be started with the name `"alexander"` using the provided `conf.yaml` configuration. Once the instance is running, connect to it at `127.0.0.1:3301` with the appropriate credentials and capture the connection output to `/app/result.txt`.

The file `/app/result.txt` must contain the output produced when connecting to the Tarantool instance at `127.0.0.1:3301`.

Build and publish a Docker image tagged `bbrc:v1.0.0` using the `Dockerfile` at `/app/Dockerfile`. Run an efficiency audit using `wagoodman/dive` with `--ci --lowestEfficiency=0.9` and save the full output to `/app/dive_result.txt`.

Set up a local Docker registry, push the image to it, and verify the push by pulling the image back from the registry. Write `push_verified` to `/app/push_result.txt` after successful verification.

Your task is to configure a container network and ensure a specific container is running. 

The system must have a network namespace named `project` connected to a host bridge named `project0`. The `project0` bridge must be active and assigned the IP address `192.168.0.1/24`. Inside the `project` namespace, the connecting network interface must be named `eth1`, configured with the IP address `192.168.0.2/24`, and have a default route pointing to `192.168.0.1`.

Along with this network configuration, a runc container named `project` must be executing in the background.

Your task is to prepare a basic runc container environment in the `/app` directory and configure a custom network namespace. Extract a `busybox` Docker container's filesystem into `/app/rootfs` and generate a default runc specification at `/app/config.json`.

You must also set up a network namespace named `runc` connected to the host via a veth pair. The host side of the connection should be attached to a new bridge named `runc0` that is configured with the IP address `192.168.0.1/24`. Inside the `runc` namespace, the network interface must be named `eth1`, assigned the IP address `192.168.0.2/24`, and configured with a default route pointing to `192.168.0.1`. Ensure all involved network interfaces are brought up.

Capture the output of the `ip a` command executed inside the `runc` network namespace and save it to `/app/netns_config.txt`.

Set up a minimal OCI container runtime environment using `runc` with custom networking inside `/app/bundle`.

The bundle at `/app/bundle` must contain a valid OCI runtime specification (`config.json`) with a fully populated busybox `rootfs/` directory. The container process should run busybox `httpd` serving on port 8080 from `/www` inside the rootfs (with a `/www/index.html` containing `ok`). The container must use a dedicated network namespace at `/var/run/netns/runc`, and `process.terminal` must be `false`.

Networking: create a Linux bridge `runc0` (192.168.0.1/24), a veth pair (`veth-host`/`veth-guest`), attach `veth-host` to the bridge, move `veth-guest` into the `runc` network namespace, rename it to `eth1`, assign 192.168.0.2/24, and set the default route via 192.168.0.1. Then launch the container with `runc run demo`.

Cherry-pick commit `f2de8475fc4703d03a2ecc2cda627b017202e623` from the upstream `rust-windowing/winit` repository into the local Cargo-managed checkout of neovide's forked `winit` dependency, then verify the patched neovide still builds and its tests pass.

The neovide repository is at `/home/user/Git/neovide`. It depends on a fork of `winit` from `https://github.com/neovide/winit` (branch `new-keyboard-all`, pinned to commit `27967af6`), which Cargo has checked out under `~/.cargo/git/checkouts/`. In that checkout, add `https://github.com/rust-windowing/winit.git` as a remote called `upstream`, fetch it, and cherry-pick the specified commit. The cherry-picked changes should be present in the working tree (not necessarily committed).

After applying the patch, return to the neovide directory, rebuild the project, and run `cargo test` to confirm all unit tests still pass. Write the full `cargo test` output to `/app/cargo_test_output.txt`.

Build the CZICheck project located at `/app/CZICheck` from source on Linux, including its test suite. The project uses CMake and requires any necessary system dependencies to be installed before building.

Once the build is complete, run the full test suite and capture all output (both stdout and stderr) to `/app/result.txt`. The file should contain the complete verbose test execution log as produced by the test runner.

Use zinit to install and build two GitHub plugins from source: `Pirito10/Tic-Tac-Toe` and `GabrielZuany/TicTacToe`. Both plugins contain C source code that must be compiled into executable binaries using their respective Makefiles. The expected compiled binary for `Pirito10/Tic-Tac-Toe` is located at `~/.zinit/plugins/Pirito10---Tic-Tac-Toe/Tic-Tac-Toe`, and for `GabrielZuany/TicTacToe` at `~/.zinit/plugins/GabrielZuany---TicTacToe/Source_Code/exe`. Both binaries must exist and be executable after the build process.

Once both plugins are built, create `/app/result.txt` listing each plugin and the absolute path to its compiled binary. Each line should follow the format `Name: /absolute/path/to/binary`, with one entry per plugin in the order `Pirito10/Tic-Tac-Toe` then `GabrielZuany/TicTacToe`.

Using `runc` and a busybox OCI bundle rooted at `/home/user/gl3/`, set up a containerized HTTP server with custom networking. The container's process should run a `nc`-based server on port 8080 that responds with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and body `Version 1.0.0`. Configure `config.json` to use the named network namespace `/var/run/netns/runc`.

The host networking must connect the container via a bridge `runc0` at `10.10.0.1/30` and a veth pair named `veth-host` (host side, attached to bridge) and `veth-guest` (container side, at `10.10.0.2/30` inside the `runc` network namespace).

The task is complete when the container is running, a request to `http://10.10.0.2:8080` returns the expected response, and the full HTTP response (headers and body) is saved to `/home/user/gl3/http_response.txt`.

Set up a Kubernetes cluster using K3s with Calico as the CNI and Kata Containers installed via kata-deploy. Configure `kubectl` access for the `ubuntu` user at `~/.kube/config`.

Configure Calico with the pod network CIDR `10.244.32.0/19`. Install Kata Containers using the kata-deploy method from the official kata-containers repository (`https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers.git`, cloned to `/home/ubuntu/kata-containers`) and register all available Kata runtime classes with the cluster.

Validate the installation by deploying nginx workloads using the `kata-qemu` and `kata-dragonball` runtime classes using the example manifests from the kata-deploy repository. The task is complete when both deployments have pods in Running state with the `kata-deploy` DaemonSet pod also Running in the `kube-system` namespace.

Verify that the `check.sh` script in the working directory correctly manages SSH public key deployment on a remote server. The script should ensure that all public keys found in the `current/` directory are present in the server's `authorized_keys`, and that all public keys found in the `outdated/` directory are absent from it — adding any missing keys and removing any that should no longer be authorized.

Validate the script's behavior by placing a public key file (`ssh-rsa testfortheasciinemarecording`) into `current/` and running `check.sh` to confirm the key gets deployed. Then move that key file into `outdated/` and run `check.sh` again to confirm the key is removed from the server. Finally, remove the key file from `outdated/` entirely and run `check.sh` once more to confirm the script handles an empty `outdated/` directory without errors.

Save the combined output of all three `check.sh` invocations to `/app/check.log` so the results can be reviewed. The end state should be a working `check.sh` that leaves the server's `authorized_keys` consistent with the contents of `current/` and `outdated/` after each invocation, with no residual test keys remaining on the server after the final run.

Clone the `ezpz` library from `https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz` into a timestamped subdirectory under `/root/tmp/polaris-talk/`. Use the format `YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS` (e.g. `2026-04-08-143211`) for the timestamped directory name. Install CPU-only PyTorch, then install the cloned package in editable mode.

Run `python3 -m ezpz.examples.test` with a single-process CPU distributed backend (gloo). Save all output to a file named `ezpz-test-dist-DDP.log` inside the timestamped working directory.

The task is complete when `/root/tmp/polaris-talk/<timestamp>/ezpz-test-dist-DDP.log` exists and contains evidence of a successful training run: rank/backend information and per-iteration loss or throughput values.

Set up a working [Eleventy (11ty)](https://www.11ty.dev/) static site in `/app` that builds successfully. The site should be named "MadMode" and represent Dan Connolly's tinkering lab notebook.

The project must include a `package.json` with Eleventy as a dependency and build scripts, an `.eleventy.js` configuration file pointing to `src` as the input directory and `_site` as the output directory, a Nunjucks layout template at `src/_includes/layout.njk` that wraps pages with a site header (displaying the site name and tagline), main content area, and footer, a homepage at `src/index.njk` that lists posts from the `posts` collection in reverse order, and at least one post under `src/posts/` tagged as `posts` with front matter including a title, date, and layout reference. Running the build must produce the compiled site in `/app/_site`, including `/app/_site/index.html` and a rendered HTML file for the first post.

Run the `gendiff` CLI tool (installed from the project at `/app/python-project-50`) against two pairs of fixture files and capture the combined output. The tool must be built, installed, and executable as `gendiff` on the system path.

Produce a single file at `/app/result.txt` containing the plain diff output for the JSON fixture pair (`tests/fixtures/file1s.json` vs `tests/fixtures/file2s.json`) followed immediately by the plain diff output for the YAML fixture pair (`tests/fixtures/file1s.yml` vs `tests/fixtures/file2s.yml`), with no separator between them. The output format produced by `gendiff` for each pair should be its default diff representation.

Install `coniferest` version 0.0.15 with its `datasets` extra. Using the `ztf_m31` dataset, run anomaly detection with `coniferest.isoforest.IsolationForest` (random_seed=42), `sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest` (random_state=42), and `coniferest.pineforest.PineForest` (random_seed=42). Update the PineForest model using `fit_known` to incorporate label feedback. Run an active learning `Session` (from `coniferest.session`) using PineForest and a `TerminateAfter(4)` callback. Finally, load the `plasticc_gp` dataset and run `create_oracle_session` (from `coniferest.session.oracle`) with PineForest (random_seed=42) and max_iterations=20.

Save your results to `/app/results.json` with the following fields:
- `coniferest_version`: the installed version string
- `ztf_m31_data_shape`: shape of the data array as `[rows, cols]`
- `ztf_m31_metadata_shape`: shape of the metadata array as `[rows]`
- `coniferest_isoforest_argmin`: argmin index from `coniferest` IsolationForest scores
- `sklearn_isoforest_argmin`: argmin index from `sklearn` IsolationForest scores
- `pineforest_argmin`: argmin index from PineForest scores
- `pineforest_fit_known_scores_shape`: length of the score array after calling `fit_known`
- `session_known_labels_count`: number of labeled items after the Session terminates
- `oracle_session_known_labels_count`: number of labeled items after the OracleSession completes
- `oracle_session_cumsum`: cumulative count of anomaly labels (label == -1) across the 20 iterations, as a list of integers

Build the MISA-MD molecular dynamics simulation package from source. The source archive is located at `/app/online1/misamd.tgz` and should be extracted and built inside `/app/online2/MISA-MD/`.

The build must use MPI compilers (`mpicc`/`mpicxx`). Dependencies should be resolved using the project's package manager before configuring and compiling. The final compiled binary should be produced inside `/app/online2/MISA-MD/build/`.

Use the `dockdiver` tool located in `~/dockdiver` to interact with a local Docker registry. Build the tool, then use it to list available repositories and dump the contents of the `test-ubuntu` image from the registry running at `localhost`.

After dumping the image, collect all files extracted under `~/dockdiver/docker_dump/test-ubuntu`, sorted by their full paths, and write that sorted list to `/app/result.txt`. Each line in `/app/result.txt` should be the absolute path of one file found within the dumped image directory.

Implement a Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) calculator in ARM64 assembly that computes the GCD of two hardcoded numbers (48 and 18) using the Euclidean algorithm.

The source file must be located at `/app/mcd.s` and compiled into an executable at `/app/mcd`. When executed, the program must print output to stdout in the following exact format:

```
Calculando MCD de 48 y 18
El MCD es: 6
```

The program should exit cleanly with exit code 0 after printing the result.

Create an ARM64 assembly program that counts down from a given number. The program should be written in `/app/conteo_atras.s` and a `Makefile` should be present in `/app` to assemble and link it using `as` and `ld`, producing an executable at `/app/conteo_atras`.

When executed, the program must print `Cuenta atrás desde: 10` followed by a newline, then count down from 10 to 0 (inclusive), printing each number on its own line, and finally print `¡Cuenta regresiva completada!` followed by a newline. The starting value (10) must be stored as a `.quad` value in the `.data` section of the assembly source.

Create an ARM64 Assembly program that converts a user-specified number of hours to seconds. The program should prompt the user with the message `Por favor, introduce el número de horas(enteras): `, read an integer from standard input, compute the equivalent number of seconds (multiplying by 3600), and print the result followed by ` segundos.` and a newline.

The source file must be located at `/app/horas_seg.s` and compiled into an executable at `/app/horas_seg` using the ARM64 assembler and linker. The final binary must run correctly on an ARM64 (AArch64) Linux system, accepting a number of hours via stdin and printing the result to stdout in the format `<seconds> segundos.` (for example, given input `2`, the output should be `7200 segundos.`).

You are working in a local git repository for your CS course and need to integrate your homework from the `cslab` remote. The university's repository history is notoriously messy, requiring a specific commit tree structure to be formed.

Your objective is to update your current branch to include two specific merges: a merge of the `cs400` branch from the `cslab` remote, and a subsequent merge of the `cslab/cs400` remote-tracking branch after it has been rebased onto your local `cs400` branch. The final state of your repository must reflect this exact git history, and the homework environment must be fully initialized by executing the `bin/init-subtree` and `bin/fetch-heads` scripts.

Your task is to install the `dashing` Python package from its GitHub repository (`https://github.com/FedericoCeratto/dashing.git`) into the `/app` directory. 

To verify the installation, you must create a file at `/app/version.txt` containing the installed version of the package. The contents of this file must strictly follow the format `dashing versión <version>` (e.g., `dashing versión 0.1.0`).

Demonstrate that multiple programming languages are installed and functional on the system by running a "Hello World" program in each language and collecting all output into a single file at `/app/result.txt`.

The file `/app/result.txt` must contain exactly the following lines, in this order:

```
Hola Mundo desde Python
Hola Mundo en C++
Hola Mundo en Java
Hola Mundo en C#
Hola Mundo en Node.js
Hola Mundo en Go
Hola Mundo en Rust
Hola Mundo en PHP
```

Each line is the standard output produced by a working "Hello World" program written in Python, C++, Java, C#, JavaScript (Node.js), Go, Rust, and PHP respectively. All eight languages must be installed and their programs must execute successfully to produce this output.
